rect.title: This diagram is drawn from ply.yaml, the file describing this codebase's architecture and verification claims. Each box is a component; chips are functions with their declared checks; arrows are permitted calls (solid) and data flows (dashed); red bars are forbidden calls. A box's grey depth is how strongly it promises to be checked — white means something inside promises nothing, deeper grey means stronger checks promised, and the weakest function sets the whole box's shade. Nothing here is green: green is kept for evidence a run has actually earned, which this render never sees, so a picture full of promises should not look like a picture full of results. Hover anything for its meaning.

g.title: ply.yaml — the document this picture is drawn from. Everything you see here was declared in it; nothing was inferred from code. What each box has actually been checked for is what `cargo ply verify` reports, not this drawing. ply: 1 — the format version every rule below is read under; a version this build does not speak is refused, never guessed at

What this document declares. "0 functions promise nothing" counts functions that end up with nothing checked -- whether nobody wrote any checks for them, or the document switched checking off for them on purpose. Running `cargo ply verify` is what turns promises into results; this line never reports results.

component intake — maps to Rust module settlement::intake state Instruction — this document asks to show id, amount_cents, received_at, and none of them declare a shape of their own, so none is drawn: a bare name carries no shape, and there is no code here to read one from either promises nothing as a whole — something inside declares no checks, and one unchecked thing sets the level of everything around it (unclaimed) hollow — promises nothing yet: no functions, no nested components. Saying what it holds is not a promise about how it behaves. Nothing to zoom into; a sketch waiting for claims.

component ledger — maps to Rust module settlement::ledger owns Ledger — only this component may mutate them state Ledger — the structure this component holds, where `owns` says who may change one. The rows below are its fields, as the document declares them: there is no code here yet to check those declarations against. Once the code exists, it decides what gets drawn and each declaration is only checked against it declares checks up to bounded — proved for every input up to a loop bound — the strongest verdict this could earn if every declared check ran and passed; a promise, never a result this box is this shade because `Ledger::post` is the weakest thing in it: it declares bounded — proved for every input up to a loop bound — nothing here is drawn stronger than its weakest part

by_account — one of the things this component holds; the narrow cell beside a wide one, twice, means a lookup table: you hand it a key and it gives you back a value. This shape was declared by the document: there is no code here yet to check it against. Once the code exists, the source decides what gets drawn here and this declaration is only checked against it, never drawn over it.

queued — one of the things this component holds; the three stacked bars mean a list: many values, kept in the order they were put in. This shape was declared by the document: there is no code here yet to check it against. Once the code exists, the source decides what gets drawn here and this declaration is only checked against it, never drawn over it.

last_settled — one of the things this component holds; the dashed outline means the value might not be there at all. This shape was declared by the document: there is no code here yet to check it against. Once the code exists, the source decides what gets drawn here and this declaration is only checked against it, never drawn over it.

total_cents — one of the things this component holds; the filled block means one single value -- a number, a flag, a character. This shape was declared by the document: there is no code here yet to check it against. Once the code exists, the source decides what gets drawn here and this declaration is only checked against it, never drawn over it.

Ledger::post bounded(2) — Kani symbolically checks supported inputs that satisfy requires against ensures; 2 is the maximum loop-unwind depth, not a numeric input limit; collection inputs may also be limited to length 2

component dedupe — maps to Rust module settlement::dedupe pure — the double border is the seal: this component declares no capabilities and may not use any. That is declared here, and not checked by this build: Ply currently compares crate-level dependencies and does not yet look inside functions, so capability use inside this sealed component can still go unnoticed (§5.3) state SeenIds — the structure this component holds. The rows below are its fields, as the document declares them: there is no code here yet to check those declarations against. Once the code exists, it decides what gets drawn and each declaration is only checked against it declares checks up to bounded — proved for every input up to a loop bound — the strongest verdict this could earn if every declared check ran and passed; a promise, never a result this box is this shade because `SeenIds::admit` is the weakest thing in it: it declares bounded — proved for every input up to a loop bound — nothing here is drawn stronger than its weakest part

seen — one of the things this component holds; the three loose circles mean a set: each value appears once, and there is no order to them. This shape was declared by the document: there is no code here yet to check it against. Once the code exists, the source decides what gets drawn here and this declaration is only checked against it, never drawn over it.

SeenIds::admit bounded(3) — Kani symbolically checks supported inputs that satisfy requires against ensures; 3 is the maximum loop-unwind depth, not a numeric input limit; collection inputs may also be limited to length 3 fuzz(64) — tries 64 generated inputs that satisfy requires, then checks ensures

component reporting — maps to Rust module settlement::reporting state Report — the structure this component holds. The rows below are its fields, as the document declares them: there is no code here yet to check those declarations against. Once the code exists, it decides what gets drawn and each declaration is only checked against it. It also asks to show cursor, which declares no shape of its own, so no row is drawn for it: a bare name carries no shape, and there is no code here to read one from promises nothing as a whole — something inside declares no checks, and one unchecked thing sets the level of everything around it (unclaimed) hollow — promises nothing yet: no functions, no nested components. Saying what it holds is not a promise about how it behaves. Nothing to zoom into; a sketch waiting for claims.

intake -> ledger — intake may call ledger. That an undeclared cross-component call is forbidden is declared here, and not checked by this build: Ply currently compares crate-level dependencies and does not yet look inside functions, so a call that crosses this line can still go unnoticed (§5.3)

ledger -> dedupe — ledger may call dedupe. That an undeclared cross-component call is forbidden is declared here, and not checked by this build: Ply currently compares crate-level dependencies and does not yet look inside functions, so a call that crosses this line can still go unnoticed (§5.3)

ledger -> reporting — ledger may call reporting. That an undeclared cross-component call is forbidden is declared here, and not checked by this build: Ply currently compares crate-level dependencies and does not yet look inside functions, so a call that crosses this line can still go unnoticed (§5.3)
